event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late-night Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) tracked southeastward through central Iowa from the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th. This line of storms moved through a highly unstable environment, characterized by CAPE values of 4000 to 5000 J/kg. Effective wind shear was also favorable for organized severe weather, with 35 to 45 kts of shear ahead of the line. The structure of the system allowed areas along the eastern fringe, tracking east-southeastward, to remain balanced with the environment and produce strong winds across northern Iowa. Widespread crop, tree, and powerline damage was reported from straight-line winds throughout Winnebago, Hancock, Cerro Gordo, and Worth counties. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Social media report of tree limbs down across Ledyard.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Report of 80 mph wind gust.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station gust to 62 mph. Widespread tree damage and minor sheet metal damage through the town of Ruthven just south of this station.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late-night Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) tracked southeastward through central Iowa from the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th. This line of storms moved through a highly unstable environment, characterized by CAPE values of 4000 to 5000 J/kg. Effective wind shear was also favorable for organized severe weather, with 35 to 45 kts of shear ahead of the line. The structure of the system allowed areas along the eastern fringe, tracking east-southeastward, to remain balanced with the environment and produce strong winds across northern Iowa. Widespread crop, tree, and powerline damage was reported from straight-line winds throughout Winnebago, Hancock, Cerro Gordo, and Worth counties. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large tree branches down in Urbandale due to collapsing storm.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge was in place across the area, creating a hot and humid environment that was deeply unstable with MLCAPE of 3000-4500 J/kg even through the overnight hours when storms passed across Iowa. Sub-severe storms developed on the evening of July 29th associated with a stationary boundary that was draped across the state, but with little available shear they were disorganized. Meanwhile, a shortwave riding along the ridge pushed in from the west and reached western Iowa after midnight. This upper level support helped to organize the earlier convection into a line of storms in eastern Iowa while the primary line of storms organized in western Iowa. Both resulted in winds gusting 55-65+ mph as they swept across the state, leaving behind broken and uprooted trees that damaged homes in a couple cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large hardwood tree uprooted and fell on home. Delayed Report. Time estimated from  radar.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of July 29, 2026, a surface front draped from central Nebraska to the state's northeast and southeastern South Dakota, serving as the focal point for thunderstorm development during the late afternoon. As the evening progressed, these storms coalesced into a mesoscale convective complex (MCS) that moved southeast across eastern Nebraska and southwestern Iowa. While the atmosphere was primed with sufficient instability, a lack of shear remained a limiting factor for widespread storm organization. Regardless, several reports of damaging wind gusts ranging from 58 to 70 mph were received throughout the evening. A notable report came from a trained spotter 3 miles west of Westphalia, Iowa, who measured a 70 mph gust. Damage was also reported, including 6- to 8-inch diameter tree limbs downed in Murray, Nebraska.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trained spotter measured wind gust using a handheld anemometer. Had consistent 45-55 mph gusts and one gust of 70 mph.

Sub-severe storms developed on the evening of July 29th associated with a stationary boundary that was draped across the state, but with little available shear they were disorganized. Meanwhile, a shortwave riding along the ridge pushed in from the west and reached western Iowa after midnight. This upper level support helped to organize the earlier convection into a line of storms in eastern Iowa while the primary line of storms organized in western Iowa. Both resulted in winds gusting 55-65+ mph as they swept across the state, leaving behind broken and uprooted trees that damaged homes in a couple cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 68 mph gust at a Personal Weather Station.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines down around Fort Dodge. Delayed report relayed by broadcast media. Time estimated by radar.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late-night Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) tracked southeastward through central Iowa from the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th. This line of storms moved through a highly unstable environment, characterized by CAPE values of 4000 to 5000 J/kg. Effective wind shear was also favorable for organized severe weather, with 35 to 45 kts of shear ahead of the line. The structure of the system allowed areas along the eastern fringe, tracking east-southeastward, to remain balanced with the environment and produce strong winds across northern Iowa. Widespread crop, tree, and powerline damage was reported from straight-line winds throughout Winnebago, Hancock, Cerro Gordo, and Worth counties. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Corn stalks blown over and tree limbs down.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)

EVENT_NARRATIVE: The public reported pine trees down near Decorah.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Buena Vista, Cerro Gordo, Clay, Dickinson, Lyon, Palo Alto, Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms rapidly developed across northeast South Dakota into west central Minnesota during the early evening of July 27 within a volatile environment (MUCAPE 5000-6000 J/Kg) ahead of a southward moving surface boundary. These thunderstorms expanded into a mesoscale convective system and dropped south across the region through the remainder of the evening into the early overnight hours on July 28. Most reported wind gusts ranged from 55 to 65 mph with one location reporting a gust to 70 mph. Isolated tree damage was also observed across northwest Iowa, along with some urban flooding in Sheldon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 70 mph wind gust was measured at the Woodbury County Fairgrounds.

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on July 17, 2025 (Hancock County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Two distinct supercell clusters developed across central South Dakota during the late afternoon of July 28 within a highly unstable environment (MUCAPE up to 5000 J/kg) ahead of an eastward advancing surface front. The southern supercell cluster produced three tornadoes across Gregory County, the strongest of which was rated EF2. ||Scattered severe wind gusts were reported across southeast South Dakota as the thunderstorms moved east before the two clusters merged near and south of Sioux Falls. Aided by increasing deep layer shear from the north, a linear structure rapidly developed with a derecho racing eastward into northwest Iowa. Winds gusted from 80 to 100 mph along the derecho's path with widespread tree and structural damage across the area. In addition, three embedded short-lived tornadoes were documented within the line of thunderstorms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at Storm Lake Municipal Airport (KSLB).

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on July 17, 2025 (Hancock County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal Weather Station gust to 59 mph.

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on July 17, 2025 (Hancock County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A thermal ridge was in place across the area, creating a hot and humid environment that was deeply unstable with MLCAPE of 3000-4500 J/kg even through the overnight hours when storms passed across Iowa. Sub-severe storms developed on the evening of July 29th associated with a stationary boundary that was draped across the state, but with little available shear they were disorganized. Meanwhile, a shortwave riding along the ridge pushed in from the west and reached western Iowa after midnight. This upper level support helped to organize the earlier convection into a line of storms in eastern Iowa while the primary line of storms organized in western Iowa. Both resulted in winds gusting 55-65+ mph as they swept across the state, leaving behind broken and uprooted trees that damaged homes in a couple cases.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 mph gust at a personal weather station.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Early on July 28, 2025, a mesoscale convective system (MCS) tracking south across Iowa triggered a brief period of damaging winds in extreme eastern Nebraska and southwestern Iowa. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Plymouth County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Plymouth County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station gust to 62 mph. Widespread tree damage and minor sheet metal damage through the town of Ruthven just south of this station.

event_description: Severe Weather occurring on July 28, 2025 and continuing (Plymouth County)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A late-night Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) tracked southeastward through central Iowa from the night of July 27th into the morning of July 28th. This line of storms moved through a highly unstable environment, characterized by CAPE values of 4000 to 5000 J/kg. Effective wind shear was also favorable for organized severe weather, with 35 to 45 kts of shear ahead of the line. The structure of the system allowed areas along the eastern fringe, tracking east-southeastward, to remain balanced with the environment and produce strong winds across northern Iowa. Widespread crop, tree, and powerline damage was reported from straight-line winds throughout Winnebago, Hancock, Cerro Gordo, and Worth counties. Thunderstorm wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph were measured, with a 71 mph wind gust at the Mason City Municipal Airport.|The portion of the line tracking more southward was oriented from east to west. This orientation was less favorable for system organization, as the wind shear vectors were parallel to the cold pool. Consequently, this portion of the line quickly became outflow-dominant, which limited the threat of widespread wind damage. However, the environment remained conducive for strong downburst winds, which occurred sporadically as new updrafts developed along the line through north-central into central Iowa. Many of these downbursts were near or slightly below severe limits, generally producing small tree branch damage, including within the Des Moines metro area. However, pockets of severe winds causing tree damage still occurred within this less organized portion of the storm.|Behind the initial line, a few clusters of storms oriented from north to south tracked east-southeastward, taking advantage of a more favorable shear orientation. One of these storms produced a 66 mph wind gust in Emmet County. However, these trailing storms generally remained sub-severe as they developed in the more stable, rain-cooled air behind the initial MCS.|After reaching Interstate 80 around 2:00 AM on July 28th, the storms became disorganized, and only general, non-severe thunderstorms continued southward through the remainder of the morning.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A derecho moved across northern Iowa, resulting in a swath of wind damage with gusts of 60 to 80 mph reported, along with two tornadoes that occurred along the leading edge of the line of storms. The line of storms developed with an embedded shortwave that rode over a larger upper level ridge. That ridge allowed for hot and humid conditions across the area with temperatures in the upper 80s to low 90s and dewpoints in the 70s, resulting in heat indicies well over 100. This made for a deeply unstable airmass with over 5000 J/kg of MLCAPE and the line of storms rode the CAPE gradient across northern Iowa overnight. With 30-35 kts of 0-6 km shear, convection was able to maintain strength, and 0-3 km shear near 25 kts orthognal to the line was able to provide just enough of a tornadic set up. The line of storms reach western portions of the area by around 11 pm local time and finally exited east just after 2 am local time. Widespread tree damage and power outages were reported with this line of storms.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees and powerlines down around Fort Dodge. Delayed report relayed by broadcast media. Time estimated by radar.

event_description: Severe Weather and Flooding occurring on August 17, 2025 (Chickasaw, Winnebago, Winneshiek Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak shortwave moved across Iowa overnight and through the morning of August 18th. And line of storms with trailing stratiform area passed across the state with the wave through the morning. MLCAPE was around 1500-2000 J/kg with a weak 850 mb low level jet sustaining storms. With weak effective shear around 20 kts or less, storms struggled to organize and did not become severe. As storms moved east, there was a pocket of enhanced low level stability with around 100 J/km of 0-3 km CAPE. This was enough to incur low level stretching and result in a few tornadoes in Grundy County. Tornadoes remained in open cropland and did not result in any structural or tree damage, identified by drone and satellite imagery.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Drone imagery provided by the emergency manager and satellite imagery revealed a track in agricultural fields. No DIs were impacted, resulting in an EF-U rating.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on April 13 and continuing(Carroll, Crawford, Grundy, Harrison, and Washington Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms impacted eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa on April 23rd, 2026. The system was driven by a broad upper-level trough located over the western third of the United States, as additional shortwave energy rounded the ridge and pushed into the central Plains. In response to these features, strong lee troughing developed across the Great Plains. Southerly winds rapidly drew rich Gulf moisture northward, pushing dewpoints into the 60s. Surface observations showed a front draped from south-central Nebraska into northeast Nebraska and northwest Iowa, which slowly progressed eastward through the afternoon. This system brought strong winds throughout the vertical column, increasing deep-layer shear. This enhanced shear combined with steep lapse rates to provide a highly favorable environment for severe thunderstorms. A weak cap in place during the afternoon initially limited development until a few convective updrafts managed to punch through. The initial storms were isolated, posing a primary threat for large hail and tornadoes, particularly for those that interacted with the frontal boundary. Through the late afternoon and into the evening, convective development became much more widespread along the front as it slowly pushed eastward, bringing reports of hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes. ||Numerous hail reports were received throughout the event. As storms matured, a southwest-to-northeast oriented broken line of supercells formed, extending generally from Lincoln, NE, through Omaha, NE, and into Little Sioux, IA. Wind gusts were measured up to 68 mph, and a tornado was confirmed near Little Sioux as a supercell approached the frontal boundary and underwent a storm merger. Within this corridor, hail ranging from 1 to 1.75 inches in diameter was widely reported. Further south, an additional strong supercell developed near Fairbury, NE. This storm tracked east-northeast, gradually growing upscale as it advanced. As the cell progressed, it produced hail up to 2 inches in diameter and spawned three brief tornadoes in southwest Iowa.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video and photo evidence of a small tornado near this location.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on May 15 and continuing(Emmet, Hancock, Palo Alto, Plymouth, Pocahontas, Winnebago, Woodbury, and Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind gust measured by the AWOS station KSLB at the Storm Lake Airport.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on May 15 and continuing(Emmet, Hancock, Palo Alto, Plymouth, Pocahontas, Winnebago, Woodbury, and Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds gusts and hail across southwest Iowa. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska, eventually pushing into southwest Iowa by 4:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster.||The primary hazards with this portion of the severe complex were large hail and significant straight-line winds. Residents in communities such as Farragut and College Springs reported hail up to ping-pong ball size (1.50 inches). Meanwhile, the bowing segments of the storm complex continued to produce extreme downdrafts, highlighted by an 84 mph wind gust measured by a personal weather station northeast of Shambaugh. The storms tracked eastward into the evening hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency management report of hail measured up to 1.50 inches in diameter.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on May 15 and continuing(Emmet, Hancock, Palo Alto, Plymouth, Pocahontas, Winnebago, Woodbury, and Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts across southwest Iowa on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. As the severe squall line pushed across the Missouri River into western Iowa during the mid-to-late evening hours of May 17, it maintained its intensity and continued to produce damaging straight-line winds. Personal weather stations across the region captured a series of severe gusts as the system swept eastward. Early in the evening, a 62 mph gust was measured near Rodney in Monona County, followed shortly by a 65 mph gust near Missouri Valley in Harrison County. As the storms progressed further southeast, the winds remained severe, with a 60 mph gust recorded near Oakland in Pottawattamie County and a localized peak gust of 72 mph measured southeast of Henderson in Montgomery County before the complex eventually exited the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Personal weather station measured wind gust of 65 mph.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on May 15 and continuing(Emmet, Hancock, Palo Alto, Plymouth, Pocahontas, Winnebago, Woodbury, and Worth Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: As a strong wave sheared northward through the Dakotas, the right entrance region of an upper level jet interacted with a slow moving surface boundary to increase late day backing of wind fields and convergence.  While overall thermodynamic parameters were lacking, favorable overlap of near-surface vorticity and acceleration of near-surface parcels resulted in low-level rotating storms.  One storm anchored near the boundary produced a brief tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A very brief tornado touchdown was documented by two independent photos. The tornado  spun up briefly in open areas between the Little Sioux River and Morgan Trail to the north of Oto.  After traveling north for less than a minute, the tornado lifted just prior to crossing Morgan Trail.  The average path width was estimated at 30 yards.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on May 15 and continuing(Cherokee, Clay, Kossuth, Montgomery, and Ringgold Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak wave in northwest flow aloft enhanced the low-level jet into southeast South Dakota with moisture and better deep-layer shear arriving by late day near a weak frontal boundary. With mixed-layer instability from 1500-2200 J/kg and marginally supportive deep layer shear of 40-45 kts, isolated supercells developed with mainly hail from stronger cells up to 2 inches in diameter.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on June 5 and continuing(Adams, Dubuque, Madison, Mills, Montgomery, Page, Pottawattamie, Ringgold, Taylor, Union, and Wapello Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of June 11, 2026, severe thunderstorms pushing across southeast Nebraska into southwest Iowa produced tornadoes, large hail, damaging wind gusts, and flash flooding. The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A brief tornado developed just east of the Missouri River at approximately 4:31 AM CST. The tornado produced minor tree damage as it tracked east towards Interstate 29. As the tornado reached Interstate 29, the tornado intensified. EF1 damage was produced at a residence located along Western Ave with most of the roof lifted off this residence. The tornado then crossed Interstate 29 and produced tree damage along the interstate before dissipating at approximately 4:32 AM CST. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 110 mph.

The synoptic setup for the event featured broad upper-level troughing over the Northern High Plains, with a strong shortwave trough pushing into eastern Nebraska early in the day. This feature provided upper-level dynamic support for the amplification of the low-level jet (LLJ) alongside subsequent low-level warm air and moisture advection. This ultimately generated the forcing necessary for storm development, which began around 1:00 AM to 2:00 AM local time over central Nebraska.||As the LLJ strengthened overnight, a surface frontal boundary began to advance northward into southeast Nebraska. Isentropic upglide to the north of the surface front led to destabilization above the boundary layer. This elevated instability, combined with 40 to 55 knots of 1-3 km bulk shear along the nose of the LLJ, led to the organization of a strong mesoscale convective system (MCS) that tracked across eastern Nebraska and into southwest Iowa.||As the storms initally pushed into eastern Nebraska, the first report of large hail���measuring up to 1.25 inches in diameter���surfacing was reported in Seward County at 2:19 AM CST. By 3:00 AM CST, the system intensified and progressed eastward into Lancaster County, producing an initial 74 mph wind gust near Valparaiso and dropping hail up to 2.50 inches in diameter. As the storms tracked directly through Lancaster County between 3:11 AM and 4:01 AM CST, they generated widespread wind damage, snapping trees and downing powerlines. One notable incident occurred at 3:46 AM CST when an estimated 10-inch diameter tree limb fell onto a home, resulting in an injury. The system then continued east toward the Missouri River, pushing into Cass County around 4:04 AM CST where it immediately began causing structural damage and dropped its first reported tornadoes shortly after 4:10 AM CST.||Crossing into southwest Iowa around 4:30 AM CST, the system's focus shifted heavily toward pockets of damaging wind gusts, brief tornadoes and flash flooding. Tornadoes were reported consecutively across Fremont, Mills, Page, and Montgomery counties between 4:29 AM CST and 5:11 AM CST. As the morning progressed, intense straight-line winds up to 90 mph continued in a swatch across eastern Page and Montgomery counties in Iowa, particularly between Coburg and Villisca, IA. By 5:26 AM CST, the severe wind and hail threats began to transition into a significant flash flood event. Heavy downpours���including a staggering 6 inches of rain reported in Sidney, Iowa by 6:00 AM CST���led to flooded creeks, residential yards, and submerged roadways across Page and Fremont counties as the storms finally pushed out of the area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Mesonet measured wind gust of 73 mph.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on June 29 and continuing(Jasper, Osceola, Polk, Story Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late afternoon and evening of July 3, 2026, thunderstorms produced large hail and damaging wind gusts across eastern Nebraska and southwest Iowa. The storms initiated along an outflow boundary draped across the area, a remnant of thunderstorms from the previous night. The environment was primed with ample instability (MUCAPE around 3000 J/kg) alongside modest but sufficient bulk shear of approximately 30 knots. Thunderstorms initiated during the afternoon, initially organizing into a few supercells before eventually growing upscale into a larger convective cluster.||Initial storms that developed across eastern Nebraska during the late afternoon were pulse-like in nature. Radar trends suggested a few localized downbursts, one of which led to a report of large snapped tree limbs 3 miles southeast of Omaha, NE, at 4:10 PM CST. Heading into the evening, a few supercells developed across eastern Nebraska, producing hail up to 1.75 inches in diameter in both Otoe and Lancaster counties. A few 1.00-inch hail reports were also received in and around Gretna, NE, as another supercell developed.||Later in the evening, the convection gradually grew upscale into a larger cluster, slowly pushing southward into southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa. Additional severe hail reports were received in Syracuse, NE, and Sidney, IA, while thunderstorm winds caused tree damage through the town of Cook, NE. The storms continued into northeast Kansas and northwest Missouri late in the evening, with a final 58 mph wind gust measured by the Falls City, NE ASOS at 10:11 PM CST.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency manager report of hail measured up to 1.00 inch in diameter.

event_description: Severe Weather Occurring on July 20 and continuing(Franklin and Hardin Counties)
EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered storms developed during the very late afternoon across central South Dakota, and moved into an environment of considerable instability (>4000 J/kg MLCAPE and 40-45 knots of effective deep-layer shear). Storms congealed into a broken linear structure while spreading eastward through southeast South Dakota and into southwest Minnesota and northwest Iowa by mid to late evening. An increasing dry layer farther east allowed storms to rapidly weaken by late evening across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts were measured by a personal weather station.
